title: Testing ML Code: Unit Tests, Integration Tests and Layout

concepts.heading: Unit Tests for Notebook Functions
concepts.body: A unit test checks one small function in isolation, early and often. Databricks shows the pattern with pytest. A function should return one predictable outcome of one data type: a column check returns true or false, a row count returns a non-negative whole number, never "false, or the thing itself". Run the tests against small fake DataFrames that copy the production schema, not against production tables, because a test must never change real data. By default pytest collects files named `test_*.py` (or `*_test.py`) and functions named `test_*`, so a file `checks_features.py` with `check_age_bucket` runs zero tests. Run the tests from a notebook, because the web terminal has no Spark support: `%pip install pytest`, then `retcode = pytest.main([".", "-v", "-p", "no:cacheprovider"])` after `sys.dont_write_bytecode = True` for read-only file systems. End with `assert retcode == 0`; without it a failing test leaves the job task green. The verbose results are in the cluster driver logs. Code kept in files outside notebooks must create its own Spark session, because only notebooks inject `spark`.

concepts.heading: Which Tests Run at Which Stage
concepts.body: In the Databricks MLOps workflow the stages split the tests. In development the team writes and runs unit tests while building the pipelines. In staging, CI starts on a pull request against main: it builds the code and runs the unit tests, and a failure rejects the pull request. Integration tests then run all the pipelines together (feature engineering, training, inference and monitoring), so a hand-off fault, such as a feature pipeline writing `cust_id` while training reads `customer_id`, fails here and not in production. When tests fail, the CI/CD system should notify users and post the results on the pull request; when they pass, the code merges to main and a release branch triggers the production update. The deployment pattern decides where the final tests run: with deploy code they run in staging, with deploy models only the artifact moves, so the final code tests run in development. Code tests do not validate a model: each newly trained production version still passes the validation pipeline before it gets the Challenger alias. Development can be given access to the staging catalog to debug a failure.

concepts.heading: Designing an Integration Test for the ML Pipeline
concepts.body: An integration test exercises the whole chain of feature computation, training, evaluation, deployment and inference, so every task must really execute. Keep staging as close to production as is reasonable, with the same libraries and cluster settings, and trade fidelity for speed or cost by shrinking the data or the training iterations, never by skipping steps. A nine-hour training run becomes a run on a small sample that still logs, registers and hands the model to inference. For real-time inference, trigger the model deployment pipeline so that it creates a temporary serving endpoint in staging, and send a few requests. In practice the test loads the model URI produced by the training task of the same run, passed along as a task value, not a released alias such as `@Champion`; otherwise the test passes while the new version is never touched. The docs also suggest scheduled integration tests on main when many pull requests merge concurrently. Giving each run its own schema in the staging catalog and dropping it afterwards, so parallel pull requests do not overwrite each other, is general engineering practice rather than a documented step.

concepts.heading: Organizing Functions and Their Tests
concepts.body: Databricks describes three layouts and recommends one per language. Functions and tests stored outside notebooks (files in a Git folder) can be imported by notebooks, job script tasks and external CI, and test frameworks such as pytest are designed to run there; the costs are more files to track, and the layout is not supported for Scala. Functions in one notebook and tests in another make reuse across notebooks easy, but the functions cannot be used or tested outside notebooks. Functions and tests in the same notebook are the simplest to maintain and the hardest to reuse, which suits a one-off analysis. The recommendation: for Python and R keep functions and tests outside notebooks; for Scala keep functions in one notebook and tests in a separate notebook; for SQL define the logic as SQL user-defined functions in a schema and call them, and their test queries, from SQL notebooks. Choose by reuse need: a wheel task or an external CI runner cannot import a function that lives only in a notebook.

examPoints: Test design: one predictable return type, fake data shaped like production, `test_*` names, `assert retcode == 0` so failures fail the task, results in the driver logs, Spark tests in a notebook.
Stages: unit tests on the pull request, integration tests across all pipelines in staging; final tests run in staging for deploy code and in development for deploy models.
Layout: Python and R outside notebooks, Scala as two notebooks, SQL as SQL UDFs in a schema; functions kept in notebooks cannot be reused outside notebooks.

quiz.q: A nightly job task runs `pytest.main([".", "-v"])` in a notebook. Last night two tests failed, yet the task shows success and the release continued. What change makes failing tests stop the pipeline?
choices: Install pytest with `%pip` in a separate first cell, because a missing installation lets the test run report success by default and hides failures
Run the same command in the web terminal of the cluster, whose process exit code fails the job task whenever any single test fails
Keep the return value of `pytest.main` and assert that it equals 0, so a failing run raises an error in the cell
Add `-p no:cacheprovider` to the call, because pytest otherwise swallows assertion errors that it has cached from earlier runs of the suite
quiz.explain: `pytest.main` returns an exit code instead of raising, so the cell succeeds unless the code is checked; asserting that it is 0 turns failing tests into a failing cell and task. Installing pytest, moving to the web terminal (which has no Spark support) or disabling the cache provider do not change how failures are reported.

quiz.q: Pull request integration tests must finish quickly, but training the full model takes many hours. The team still wants the test to catch hand-off faults between the pipelines. Which design fits best?
choices: Run all pipelines in staging on a small data sample or with fewer iterations, so training, registration and inference still execute
Skip the training task and load the released Champion model, because scoring is the only stage in which a hand-off fault can appear in practice
Run only the unit tests of the training function on the pull request, since they already cover the interfaces between all of the pipelines
Run the full training in the production catalog overnight, because only production-sized data can reveal a mismatch between column names
quiz.explain: Shrinking data or iterations keeps every step executing, so a broken interface still fails within the time budget. Loading the released model never touches the candidate, unit tests isolate single functions rather than interfaces, and testing in production risks real assets without being needed to find a name mismatch.

recap: Unit tests isolate single functions with fake data and fail the task through `assert retcode == 0`; integration tests run every pipeline together in staging, with less data but no skipped steps. Final tests sit in staging for deploy code and in development for deploy models. Python and R functions live outside notebooks, SQL logic in SQL UDFs.

title: Environments and ML Assets in Declarative Automation Bundles

concepts.heading: One Environment per Stage
concepts.body: Databricks recommends a separate environment for each stage, development, staging and production, with clearly defined transitions. An environment is compute, runtimes, libraries and jobs, and it usually corresponds to one Unity Catalog catalog (dev, staging, prod). Access follows roles. Data scientists have read-write access to dev and ideally read-only access to the prod catalog, including inference and metric tables, so they can diagnose quality and compare a new model with the live one. ML engineers own production, where data scientists normally have no write or compute access. If security forbids reading prod from dev, write a snapshot of production data into the dev catalog. Code, not models, moves between stages through Git: dev branch, main after staging tests, release branch for production. Production training can use a small configured set of top hyperparameters found in dev, which saves time and reduces run-to-run variance in automated retraining. Each environment registers models in its own catalog. Creating a registered model needs `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA` and `CREATE MODEL`; adding a version needs ownership or `CREATE MODEL VERSION`.

concepts.heading: Standard Projects, Targets and Identities
concepts.body: Starting every project from the same layout is the job of the MLOps Stacks bundle template: `databricks bundle init mlops-stacks` asks whether to create `CICD_and_Project` (the default), `Project_Only` (ML code, for data scientists) or `CICD_Only` (infrastructure, for ML engineers). A bundle has targets such as dev and prod, chosen with `databricks bundle deploy -t <target>`. A target with `mode: development` prefixes deployed resources with `[dev <user>]` and pauses schedules and triggers of jobs and quality monitors. A target with `mode: production` can check the Git branch, and Databricks recommends service principals for production deployments, set with `run_as`. Pitfall: when the deploying identity differs from the `run_as` identity, only jobs and pipelines are supported, so a bundle that also holds registered models or experiments should be deployed and run by the same service principal; `run_as` is not supported for model serving endpoints at all, and defining both in one bundle is an error. Values that differ per environment, such as the catalog, come from the target, for example `catalog_name: ${bundle.target}`, so promotion deploys the same reviewed code to another target.

concepts.heading: ML Assets as Bundle Resources
concepts.body: The ML resource keys are `experiments`, `registered_models` and `model_serving_endpoints`, next to `jobs`; `models` is a legacy resource (Databricks recommends Unity Catalog `registered_models`) and `mlflow_experiments` does not exist. An experiment `name` must be an absolute workspace path, for example `/Workspace/Users/someone@example.com/my_experiment`, and a bare name fails. A registered model declares `catalog_name`, `schema_name` and `name`, plus `grants`, for example `EXECUTE` for a consuming group, which lets it load and call the model without changing it. A serving endpoint defines `config.served_entities` (`entity_name`, `entity_version`, workload settings) and a `traffic_config` with `routes`, each a `served_model_name` with a `traffic_percentage`. Two served entities routed 90 and 10 express a canary rollout inside one endpoint; the strategy is general practice, the fields are documented. `permissions` give an application `CAN_QUERY` without `CAN_MANAGE`. The `lifecycle` setting `prevent_destroy: true` stops a bundle from destroying a production registered model and its version history.

concepts.heading: Wiring Assets Together and Deploying
concepts.body: Assets in one bundle refer to each other through substitutions so that nothing is hard-coded. A training job that must log to the bundle's own experiment uses a reference of the form `${resources.experiments.<key>.id}` instead of a pasted ID, because the ID does not exist before deployment. The docs show this form for an app resource. One bundle can define the training job, the validation job, the registered model and the endpoint, so a pull request reviews pipelines and infrastructure together. A typical cycle is: `databricks bundle validate` flags unknown keys and wrong values, `databricks bundle deploy -t staging` creates the assets in the staging workspace and catalog, `databricks bundle run` starts the integration-test job, and CI repeats the deployment for prod from the release branch. Variables and targets let one YAML describe all three environments, each with its own workspace host, catalog and run identity. For fully automated workflows Databricks recommends OAuth machine-to-machine authentication with a service principal, not personal credentials.

examPoints: Environment = catalog plus workspace and jobs; data scientists get read-only access to prod (or a snapshot in dev); creating a registered model needs `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA` and `CREATE MODEL`.

Bundle ML keys: `experiments` (absolute path name), `registered_models` (`grants`), `model_serving_endpoints` (`traffic_config` routes, `CAN_QUERY`); protect production assets with `lifecycle.prevent_destroy`.

Environment differences come from targets (`${bundle.target}`), `mode` and a service principal in `run_as`; different deployer and `run_as` identities support only jobs and pipelines, and `run_as` is unsupported with serving endpoints.

quiz.q: A bundle must send 10 percent of the requests of the endpoint `churn-ep` to a new model version while the current version keeps 90 percent. How is this declared?
choices: Create a second `model_serving_endpoints` entry for the new version and ask the application team to alternate calls between both endpoint names
List two served entities with distinct names in `config.served_entities` and set `traffic_config.routes` to 90 and 10 percent
Give the endpoint a `tags` entry such as `traffic: 10` on the new version, because the router weights requests by these tags
Set `route_optimized: true` on the endpoint, since route optimization splits the incoming requests between model versions by weight
quiz.explain: Served entities with distinct names and a `traffic_config` of routes give a weighted split inside one endpoint, and the split is reviewed with the bundle. Two endpoints leave the split to the callers, tags carry billing metadata and do not route, and route optimization concerns the request path, not the traffic weights.

quiz.q: A bundle declares a registered model, an experiment and a training job. The CI user deploys it with `run_as` set to a different service principal, and the deployment of the model and the experiment is rejected. What explains this?
choices: Bundles have no `experiments` resource type, so the experiment must be created by hand, and the registered model then fails with it
The CI user needs `CREATE MODEL VERSION` on the model, a privilege that bundles cannot grant, so every deployment of a model is rejected
A `mode: development` target blocks model creation by design, and the production target creates all of these assets in a later step
With different deploying and `run_as` identities only jobs and pipelines are supported, so deploy and run as the same service principal
quiz.explain: The run-as documentation limits a bundle to jobs and pipelines when the deploying identity and the `run_as` identity differ; using one service principal for both lifts that limit for registered models and experiments. Experiments are a documented resource type, and development mode pauses schedules instead of blocking creation.

recap: One catalog and workspace per stage, code promoted through Git, data scientists read-only on prod. Bundles describe `experiments`, `registered_models` and `model_serving_endpoints` with targets, `${bundle.target}` references, grants, permissions and `prevent_destroy`; deploy and run as the same service principal when registered models or experiments are involved (serving endpoints do not support `run_as`).

title: Automated Retraining and Selecting the Top Model

concepts.heading: Scheduled Versus Triggered Retraining
concepts.body: Databricks recommends beginning with scheduled, periodic retraining on the latest data and moving to triggered retraining when needed. A trigger is a signal from monitoring: a SQL alert on the drift or profile metrics tables, for example drift or model quality against a threshold, with a webhook destination that starts the training workflow. Alternatively a job can use a table update trigger on the metric table, so it starts when fresh rows land. The run-as principal needs `SELECT` on the monitored table, and with several tables the trigger fires when any or all of them update. Two options shape the timing: minimum time between triggers and wait after last change. The docs give an example: with 120 s and 60 s, updates at 5 s and 115 s do not start a run before 115 + 60 = 175 s, because the second update restarted the 60 s wait and the 120 s minimum had already passed. A table update trigger only says that new rows exist. The profile writes drift rows at every refresh, whether or not anything drifted, so the decision to retrain needs its own gate.

concepts.heading: The Retraining Job as a Pipeline
concepts.body: Build the job from tasks: check, train, validate, deploy. A check task counts the drifted columns in the drift metrics table and publishes the count with `dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set`. An `If/else condition` task evaluates `{{tasks.check_drift.values.drifted_columns}} > 0`, and only its true branch trains, so quiet nights cost one cheap task. The operators `>` and `<` compare numbers, while `==` and `!=` compare strings, so `12.0 == 12` is false. The train task hands the registered model URI to the validate task through a task value such as `{{tasks.train.values.model_uri}}`. Asking the registry for the highest version breaks when two runs overlap, because task values are scoped to the run. Use `Run if dependencies` for a task that must also run after a failure, for example a notification. Put a data-quality gate in front of training (general practice): drift cannot tell a change in behavior from an upstream defect, such as a feature set to null for part of the rows, and retraining on that data bakes the defect into the model.

concepts.heading: What a Retraining Trigger Can and Cannot Know
concepts.body: Drift is evidence that inputs changed, not that the model got worse, so it should start a challenger and not replace the champion. When labels arrive late, say about 45 days after scoring, daily feature or prediction drift gives the early start, and the labelled evaluation against the champion decides the promotion. After an abrupt and permanent change, such as a new regulation, keep volume by weighting or flagging the old regime instead of discarding all history, and measure on a holdout from the new period. When outcomes exist only for cases the model accepted, as with approved loans, every retrain grows more confident about the applicants it already liked, so exploration or reject inference is needed before the loop can be trusted. These points are general ML practice, not a Databricks page. The docs support the pattern drift or quality alert, then retraining job, then comparison, and note that a manual approval step can be added with workflow notifications or CI/CD callbacks when full automation is not wanted.

concepts.heading: Selecting the Top Model
concepts.body: Register every retrained model as a new version, give it the Challenger alias after the validation checks, and let consumers load `models:/<catalog>.<schema>.<model>@Champion`. The Champion alias moves only when the gate passes, and batch jobs and endpoints follow without code changes. Compare champion and challenger offline on the same fresh holdout, logging both in MLflow, never against a metric stored months ago. For real-time serving a longer online comparison, such as a gradual rollout or a traffic split between served models, is possible. Choose the metric to fit the problem; the rules from here on are general practice, not Databricks documentation. With 0.4% positives, a model that always predicts the majority class has accuracy 1 - 0.004 = 99.6%, so use PR AUC or recall at the precision the review team can afford. Use log loss and calibration when probabilities enter a formula, and a time-ordered split for time-dependent data. Require a margin plus a supported difference so the alias does not flip between near-identical models, rank runs on validation metrics and score the test set once, and treat latency and signature compatibility as pass or fail gates.

examPoints: Trigger design: scheduled first; a SQL alert with a webhook or a table update trigger gives the timing; an If/else task on a task value gates the decision; task values pass the model URI to validation.
A drift alert starts a challenger; evaluation on the same fresh holdout decides; Challenger alias first, Champion alias only after the gate, and consumers load the alias.

Metric choice follows cost (general practice, not documented): PR AUC or recall at precision for rare classes, log loss for probabilities, time-ordered splits, a margin for promotion, constraints as pass or fail gates.

quiz.q: A table update trigger on the drift metrics table starts the retraining job. The profile refreshes every night and writes rows each time, so a model is trained and registered every night even when nothing drifted. What is the best fix?
choices: Replace the trigger with a cron schedule on the training job, because only scheduled jobs can combine a drift check with training inside one run
Increase the wait after last change until the nightly profile rows no longer count as a table update for the trigger on that table
Grant the run-as principal fewer privileges on the metric table, so that only rows with detected drift are visible to the trigger
Add a first task that counts drifted columns and sets a task value, then an If/else task that trains only when the count exceeds zero
quiz.explain: The trigger only reports that rows were written, so the decision to retrain must come from a gate: a task value with the drift count feeds an If/else condition and the true branch trains. A schedule has the same problem, a longer wait only delays the run, and removing privileges would make the trigger fail to evaluate instead of filtering rows.

quiz.q: A fraud model has 0.4% positive transactions. The retraining pipeline picks the challenger with the highest validation accuracy, and last month's pick missed most fraud. Analysts can review a fixed number of alerts per day. Which selection metric fits?
choices: PR AUC, or recall at the precision that the review capacity allows
Mean squared error of the predicted label on the validation set, because it weighs all rows equally and is robust to the class balance
Training accuracy of the final model, because it shows how well the model has learned the rare class from the available examples
Accuracy on a validation set from which the rare class was removed, so that every remaining row is scored with the same weight
quiz.explain: With 0.4% positives a model that never flags fraud already has 1 - 0.004 = 99.6% accuracy, so accuracy hides the failure. PR AUC and recall at a fixed precision focus on the rare class and on the alert budget. The other options either still reward the majority class, measure the training set, or remove the class that matters.

recap: Start with scheduled retraining; move to alert-and-webhook or table update triggers with an If/else gate on a task value, and a data-quality check first. Drift starts a challenger, evaluation on the same fresh holdout decides, and the Champion alias moves only after the gate. Match the metric to the cost: PR AUC for rare classes, log loss for probabilities.

title: Drift Tests, Table Types and Monitor Features

concepts.heading: The Drift Metrics Table
concepts.body: Data profiling (the feature was called Lakehouse Monitoring before the rename) writes two metric tables beside the profiled table: `{table}_profile_metrics` and `{table}_drift_metrics`. The drift table compares windows and has one row per column, window, slice and drift type. `drift_type` is `CONSECUTIVE`, which compares a window with the previous one (`window_cmp`), or `BASELINE`, which compares it with the baseline table. Baseline drift exists only if a baseline table is given, and consecutive drift only if a previous window exists. Deltas are current minus comparison, for example `avg_delta`, `percent_null_delta` and `count_delta`. Slices appear as `slice_key` and `slice_value`, with NULL for the whole table, and `column_name` is `:table` for table-level metrics such as model accuracy. A test column holds NULL where the test does not apply to the type of the column. For an inference profile a good baseline is the data the model was trained or validated on. Alerts and dashboards read these Delta tables, so a drift rule is an ordinary SQL condition on them.

concepts.heading: Which Test for Which Column
concepts.body: The drift table computes different statistics by column type. Numeric columns get `ks_test` (a struct with statistic and pvalue), `wasserstein_distance` and `population_stability_index`. Categorical columns get `chi_squared_test` (statistic and pvalue), `tv_distance`, `l_infinity_distance` and `js_distance`. A NULL `ks_test` on a categorical column is therefore not a bug. The documentation states PSI bands: below 0.1 means no significant population change, below 0.2 moderate change, and 0.2 or more significant change. Example for four device types: baseline shares 40, 30, 20 and 10 percent, current shares 30, 20, 30 and 20 percent. Every absolute difference is 0.10, so `tv_distance` = 0.5 x (0.10 x 4) = 0.20, the share of traffic that moved to other categories, while `l_infinity_distance` is the largest single difference, 0.10. Wasserstein distance is measured in the units of the feature (standard definition, not stated on the page): if every basket value rises by 12 euros, it is 12, so analysts can set limits in euros.

concepts.heading: Reading Statistical Tests Correctly
concepts.body: A p-value measures how detectable a shift is, not how important it is. With hundreds of millions of rows per window, a rule such as `ks_test.pvalue < 0.05` fires daily on shifts too small to matter, so alert on an effect size instead: the KS statistic, Wasserstein distance or PSI, with thresholds taken from business impact. Multiple testing works against you too. Testing 300 numeric features at 0.05 gives 300 x 0.05 = 15 expected false alarms per refresh even when nothing changed. Correct for the number of tests (a Bonferroni level is 0.05 / 300, about 0.00017) or alert on effect size and feature importance. Small windows fail the other way: an hourly window with about 150 requests gives jumpy statistics, so use a coarser granularity so that each estimate rests on more rows. All of this is general statistics rather than a Databricks page, but the exam expects you to pick the metric whose wording matches the policy, such as share of traffic moved (`tv_distance`) or shift in euros (Wasserstein).

concepts.heading: Choosing the Table Type and the Monitor Feature
concepts.body: Pick the profile type from the table. Snapshot suits tables without a meaningful time axis or predictions, such as a customer dimension rewritten nightly: the whole table is profiled at each refresh, and very large tables go to time series. Time series needs a timestamp column and computes metrics per window, which fits large append-only event tables. Inference fits a request log with timestamp, model id, inputs, prediction and optional label, and adds quality metrics once prediction and label are both present. Then pick the feature. Baseline drift catches slow creep: a mean rising 0.3% a day moves 1.003^42, about 1.134 (+13.4%), in six weeks, yet every daily step is small. Consecutive drift catches sudden steps, and a spike followed by recovery shows as two consecutive alerts but only one differing window against the baseline. When inputs are stable but accuracy falls (concept drift), supply the label column. With delayed labels, watch prediction drift as a label-free early signal, and use slices to inspect segments.

examPoints: Drift table: `drift_type` CONSECUTIVE versus BASELINE; numeric columns use `ks_test`, `wasserstein_distance`, `population_stability_index`; categorical columns use `chi_squared_test`, `tv_distance`, `l_infinity_distance`, `js_distance`; NULL means not applicable.
PSI bands from the docs: below 0.1 no significant change, below 0.2 moderate, 0.2 or more significant; at large sample sizes alert on effect size, and correct for multiple tests (300 x 0.05 = 15).

Snapshot for tables without time axis, time series for timestamped event tables, inference for prediction logs; baseline drift for slow creep, consecutive for sudden steps, label column for concept drift.

quiz.q: The latest window of a numeric feature has `population_stability_index` = 0.15 against the baseline. How does the data profiling documentation classify this value?
choices: Moderate population change, because it is below 0.2, the value from which the change counts as significant
No significant change, because values stay acceptable up to 0.2 and only larger values count as population drift
Significant change, because every value of 0.1 or more is flagged and 0.2 is only the limit for a moderate change
Not applicable, because the index is calculated for categorical columns only and a numeric feature returns NULL there
quiz.explain: The documented bands are below 0.1 no significant change, below 0.2 moderate change and 0.2 or more significant change, so 0.15 is moderate. The index is calculated for numeric columns, and categorical columns are the ones that return NULL.

quiz.q: A categorical feature has four device types. Baseline shares are 40%, 30%, 20% and 10%; the current window has 30%, 20%, 30% and 20%. Product wants the rule "alert when at least 15 percent of traffic has moved to other categories". Which drift column and value apply?
choices: `l_infinity_distance` with a value of 0.10, which is below 0.15, so the rule does not fire for this window
`ks_test.statistic` with a value of 0.20, which categorical columns receive after their values are encoded as numbers
`tv_distance` with a value of 0.20, above the 0.15 limit
`wasserstein_distance` with a value of 0.20, which equals the share of traffic moved and therefore exceeds the limit
quiz.explain: Total variation distance is half the sum of absolute share differences, 0.5 x 0.40 = 0.20, which is exactly the share of traffic that moved, so it is above 0.15 and the rule fires. The L-infinity distance is only the largest single difference, and KS and Wasserstein are computed for numeric columns only.

recap: The drift metrics table separates CONSECUTIVE and BASELINE comparisons and fills KS, Wasserstein and PSI for numeric columns, chi-square, total variation, L-infinity and Jensen-Shannon for categorical ones. PSI 0.1 and 0.2 are the documented bands. Use effect sizes at scale, correct for many tests, and match profile type and drift comparison to the use case.

title: Building Monitors and Monitoring Pipeline Components

concepts.heading: Creating a Profile with the SDK
concepts.body: A profile (monitor) attaches to a Unity Catalog table. The creator needs `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA`, `SELECT` and `MANAGE`, and a table can have only one profile. Install a recent SDK with `%pip install "databricks-sdk>=0.68.0"` and call `w.data_quality.create_monitor(monitor=Monitor(object_type="table", object_id=table.table_id, data_profiling_config=config))`. The config holds `output_schema_id`, `assets_dir` and one profile type: `SnapshotConfig()`, `TimeSeriesConfig(timestamp_column, granularities)` or `InferenceLogConfig(problem_type, prediction_column, model_id_column, timestamp_column, granularities, label_column)`, where the label is optional. Optional parts are `slicing_exprs`, a cron `schedule`, `notification_settings` (for example emails when a refresh fails) and custom metrics. Refresh on demand with `create_refresh`; it runs on serverless compute, not on the cluster of the notebook. Granularities range from minutes to a year and set the window size. The older `quality_monitors` API is deprecated, so build new monitors with the data quality API. Deleting a profile does not delete its metric tables or dashboard.

concepts.heading: Behavior to Expect After Creation
concepts.body: Time series and inference profiles first analyze only a recent look-back, roughly the last month, and then process all new data. A profile created today on two years of history therefore shows about a month of windows, and no error is reported. Enable change data feed on the table so that each refresh processes only the newly appended rows. A profile on a materialized view does not support incremental processing, so refresh time grows with the view; unpack the data into a Delta table with change data feed instead. A snapshot profile reprocesses the whole table at every refresh and has a size cap, so a very large append-only table with a timestamp should use a time series profile, while a dimension table rewritten nightly suits snapshot. An inference profile with a prediction column but no label column still produces drift and distribution statistics, but accuracy, precision and recall stay NULL; model quality needs both prediction and label. For classification the quality metrics include `accuracy_score`, `f1_score` and `log_loss`; for regression `root_mean_squared_error` and `r2_score`.

concepts.heading: Monitoring an Endpoint Through the Inference Table
concepts.body: The pipeline for a served model has a fixed shape. Enable an inference table on the endpoint; AI Gateway-enabled inference tables are the current option and the older endpoint inference tables are retired. The table logs raw request and response JSON with status code and timing. A scheduled job unpacks the JSON into typed feature and prediction columns according to the schema of the endpoint, joins ground-truth labels when they arrive, and writes a flat Delta table with change data feed. The inference profile attaches to that flat table, not to the raw log, because it needs one row per request with a timestamp, a model id, the inputs and the prediction. Refreshing it fills the profile and drift metric tables and the dashboard. The roles differ: the raw inference table is for row-level debugging, such as the payload, status code and execution time of one complaint, while the profile tables hold aggregated trends. Do not change the schema or name of an inference table or delete it, because logging can stop.

concepts.heading: Components of a Monitoring Pipeline
concepts.body: A complete pipeline has five parts. Logging: the inference table records requests and responses. Drift: the drift metrics table, with consecutive and baseline comparisons. Performance: quality metrics in the profile metrics table once labels are joined. Health: endpoint health metrics for latency, request rate, error rate, CPU and memory, shown in the Serving UI for a limited period; for long retention, OpenTelemetry can persist logs, metrics and traces to Unity Catalog Delta tables that SQL can query. Action: Databricks SQL alerts on the metric tables with email, webhook or chat notifications, and a retraining job behind them. Access works as for any table: the profile creator owns the metric tables, so a risk team receives `SELECT` through ordinary Unity Catalog grants. One trap: profile refresh and dashboard refresh are separate. After the profile refreshes the metric tables, the dashboard shows old charts until it is refreshed too, and refreshing the dashboard does not recompute the profile.

examPoints: Build: `data_quality.create_monitor` with `SnapshotConfig`, `TimeSeriesConfig` or `InferenceLogConfig`; needs `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA`, `SELECT` and `MANAGE`; one profile per table; label column required for quality metrics.
Large append-only tables: time series profile plus change data feed; materialized views are not processed incrementally; time series and inference profiles start with a recent look-back only.

Pipeline: inference table, unpack and label-join into a flat Delta table, inference profile, SQL alerts; row-level debugging uses the inference table, trends use the metric tables, and the dashboard refresh is separate.

quiz.q: An append-only table of clickstream events with an `event_ts` column keeps growing. A snapshot profile is rejected because the table is too large, and refresh cost must stay low. Which setup fits?
choices: A snapshot profile on a materialized view over the table, which is processed incrementally and so reads only the new events
A time series profile on `event_ts` with change data feed enabled on the table, so each refresh reads only new rows
An inference profile with `event_ts` as timestamp and the event type as prediction column, which supports tables of any size
A time series profile on a materialized view that unpacks the table, because views refresh faster than Delta tables
quiz.explain: A time series profile has no snapshot size cap and works by window on `event_ts`; change data feed lets each refresh process only appended rows. Materialized views are not processed incrementally by profiles, and an inference profile expects a prediction log, not clickstream events.

quiz.q: An inference profile refreshes on schedule and the drift tables fill normally, but accuracy, precision and recall are NULL in every window. The prediction column is configured. Which cause is most likely?
choices: The profile was created without a baseline table, which disables every accuracy-related column in the profile metrics table
Change data feed is disabled on the table, so the profile skips the quality computation and writes only the drift columns
The dashboard was not refreshed after the profile run, so the metric tables still hold the empty values from the first run
No label column with the ground truth is set, so quality metrics cannot be computed although drift statistics are
quiz.explain: Model quality needs prediction and label together; without the label column the profile still produces drift and distribution statistics. A missing baseline only removes baseline drift, change data feed affects cost and not which metrics exist, and the dashboard reads the metric tables rather than writing them.

recap: Create a profile with the SDK data quality API on a table you can manage: snapshot, time series or inference. Use time series plus change data feed for big append-only tables, flatten and label-join inference payloads before profiling, and remember the pipeline: inference table, drift, quality, endpoint health, alerts. Refresh the profile, then the dashboard.
